FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Gain skill in evaluating normal versus pathologic conditions of the foot and ankle through
physical examination.
Overview
The foot and ankle are key anatomic structures that enable individuals to walk erect with a
bipedal gait.
Both lower extremities must be evaluated to determine normal for a given patient.

Knowledge of bony, articular, muscular, tendinous, ligamentous, vascular, and neural
anatomy is essential for proficiency in physical examination. The examiner should
recognize that the foot and ankle may be considered from two perspectives. As body
parts that may manifest systemic disease (circulatory, metabolic, cutaneous) and as
constituents of the locomotor system. Asymmetry, motion, and changes in position with
gait must be evaluated. Evaluation should be performed with the patient seated and not
bearing weight and with the patient standing. (Resource 1).
General Inspection
Skin changes
Symmetry
Swelling
Atrophy
Distribution of hair

General Inspection
The presence of callus, corns, scars, rashes, blisters, or ulcers should be noted. Surface
anatomy and skin evaluation may reveal the effect extrinsic factors have had on the foot
and ankle. For example, a shoe may be too tight in a dorsal-plantar direction, causing
chronic irritation at the proximal interphalangeal joint of one of the toes. Callosity
plantar to the second and third metatarsal heads may indicate transfer metatarsalgia. A
posterior calcaneus mass—the classic Bauer bump or Haglund deformity—may cause
skin irritation and local inflammation from rubbing on shoe wear. Erythema or ulceration
may be present in a neuropathic patient because of pressure and lack of sensation. Lack
of hair distally may indicate circulatory compromise. Dry and cracked skin suggests loss
of normal sweating because of autonomic dysfunction commonly associated with
neuropathy. Moisture and blanching with ulceration in the webspace may indicate fungal
infection (athlete’s foot). Erythema may be indicative of pressure, infection, or early
Charcot arthropathy. In differentiating infection from Charcot arthropathy, elevation of
the extremity of a patient with Charcot arthropathy will cause erythema to diminish after

5 to 10 seconds, whereas erythema associated with infection will persist if the extremity

Gait Evaluation

Gait Evaluation
Gait should be observed with the patient walking toward and away from the examiner.
In evaluating gait, the surgeon must determine whether an abnormality in gait is
secondary to foot and ankle pathology or related to a more proximal issue in the
extremity. For example, a steppage gait (using the hip flexors to clear the foot in the
swing phase rather than the ankle dorsiflexors) may be related to deficiency of the
anterior tibial tendon because of neurologic dysfunction or rupture. The foot
progression angle and stride length and cadence also should be observed.
Palpation
Assess skin temperature with the dorsum of the hand or infrared thermography, if available.
Ask the patient to indicate the location of the pain.

Palpation
Gently palpate to verify areas of tenderness and correlate with pertinent anatomy. The
ligamentous and tendinous courses and their insertion sites should be evaluated. An
appropriate knowledge of anatomy is essential. Subtle bony injury, such as stress
fractures of the fifth metatarsal and the lesser metatarsal neck, may be identified by
tenderness to palpation and adjacent edema. Accurately identifying the location of
tenderness is essential. Tenderness over the dorsomedial aspect of a great toe with
hallux valgus may be related to shoe impingement on the medial eminence; however,
tenderness over the dorsolateral aspect of the hallux metatarsophalangeal joint may
indicate advancing arthritis. Tendon ruptures or abnormalities are readily palpated as a
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:44 PM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Foot and Ankle
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000027
3/25

physical defect along the line of pull of the tendon. In particular, posterior tibialis
thickening is primarily appreciated posterior to the medial malleolus, and thickening of
the Achilles tendon is appreciated approximately 4 to 6 cm proximal to the tendon
insertion. This thickening may indicate tendinosis or healing rupture. Crepitus at the
Achilles tendon with dorsiflexion and plantar flexion is indicative of paratenonitis.
Although palpation and range of motion are separate aspects of the physical
examination, joint motion aids in defining the anatomy. Subtalar motion helps identify
the sinus tarsi and the associated anterior process of the calcaneus. The talonavicular
joint supplies most forefoot adduction and abduction; therefore, moving the foot
through this motion helps identify the talonavicular joint, the insertion of the posterior
tibial tendon, and the spring ligament.

Normal passive range of motion (estimates vary between individuals and should be compared
with the unaffected extremity.
Dorsiflexion: 20°
Plantar flexion: 50°

Ankle
With the hindfoot in the neutral or valgus position, the axes of the talonavicular and
calcaneocuboid joints are parallel, which unlocks them and allows motion. With the
hindfoot inverted, the axes are skewed (not parallel), locking the hindfoot and preventing
motion. This prevents any contribution to dorsiflexion by the hindfoot and isolates ankle
motion.
This ankle is a single-axis joint with the axis of rotation just below the tips of the malleoli.
Its obliquity determines the medial and lateral deviation with plantar flexion and
dorsiflexion.
Subtalar
Normal passive range of motion is estimated. Different foot postures (cavus, planovalgus) are
associated with different capabilities of motion.
Inversion: 20°
Eversion: 10°

Range of motion is assessed most accurately with the patient in the prone position with
the knee flexed to 90°. For practical purposes, the joint may be evaluated with the
patient sitting on the examination table facing the examiner. The heel should be held in
line with the tibia with one hand cupping the malleoli and the hindfoot in the other hand
while inverting and everting the hindfoot.
Midtarsal Talonavicular and Calcaneocuboid
Normal passive range of motion
Adduction: 20°
Abduction: 10°

Midtarsal Talonavicular and Calcaneocuboid
These joints are best examined with the examiner facing the seated patient, with the
calcaneus in line with the tibia and with the plantar surface of the foot parallel to the
floor. The examiner grasps the forefoot and stabilizes hindfoot motion by grasping the
calcaneal tuberosity posteriorly.
Metatarsophalangeal Joints
Normal passive range of motion
Dorsiflexion: 45° to 90°
Plantar flexion: 10° to 40°

Semmes-Weinstein monofilament test

Sensory Examination
Loss of protective sensation, as seen in patients with diabetic neuropathy, generally is
defined by inability to sense the buckling force of a 5.07 Semmes-Weinstein nylon
monofilament. The force that this size monofilament exerts maximally with buckling is
10 g. A patient with this level of sensory loss is at increased risk for ulceration.

The patient is observed walking toward and away from the examiner on the toes and
the heels to test plantar flexion and dorsiflexion strength, respectively.

Provocative and Special Tests
The anterior talar dome is wider than the posterior dome. Therefore, if the ankle is
dorsiflexed, the fibula rotates externally and the syndesmosis, if intact, stabilizes the
joint. An unstable syndesmosis elicits a positive response to the external rotation test,
the squeeze test, and the tape stabilization test.
For the external rotation test, stabilize tibia and externally rotate the foot and ankle. A
painful response is positive for syndesmotic injury (Video 1),
Video 1 Faro FD: Video. External Rotation Test for Syndesmotic Instability. Lebanon, NH,
2023.
For the squeeze test (Video 2), medial and lateral squeezes at the mid-calf may be
painful at the distal syndesmosis. A painful response is indicative of syndesmotic injury.

The calcaneofibular ligament is the major soft-tissue structure stabilizing the ankle joint
with the ankle dorsiflexed. The anterior talofibular ligament is the major soft tissue
stabilizing the structure of the joint with the ankle plantarflexed. For the talar tilt test for
calcaneofibular ligament integrity, the patient is seated on the examination table with
the legs dangling and facing the seated examiner, and the ankle is dorsiflexed (to put the
calcaneofibular ligament on tension) and simultaneously inverted. The relative degree of
inversion is noted and compared with the opposite (unaffected) side. For the anterior
drawer test for anterior talofibular ligament integrity, the patient is seated on the
examination table with the legs dangling, and one ankle is examined at a time. The talus
and calcaneus are grasped in one hand by wrapping the fingers around the posterior
tuberosity of the ankle and the thumb over the neck of the talus. The other hand is used
to stabilize the tibia while positioning a thumb or finger at the region of the anterior
talofibular ligament to feel motion. With the hand holding the hindfoot in resting plantar
flexion (anterior talofibular ligament on tension), the foot is translated anterior and then
posterior. With the finger/thumb of the stabilizing hand, you will feel the motion allowed
by the anterior talofibular ligament. Ensure too much traction is not placed on the ankle
because this may increase perceived stability. In the unstable ankle, the examiner notes
anterior motion of the talus, an audible click may be appreciated as the dome of the
talus strikes the anterior lip of the tibia within the joint, and/or a sulcus may be observed
at the site of the anterior talofibular ligament. This phenomenon must be assessed in
the contralateral ankle joint (Video 3).
The tendons of the gastrocnemius (origin: distal femur) and the soleus (origin: proximal
tibia) join to form the Achilles tendon, which inserts at the calcaneal tuberosity. The
Silfverskiöld test for gastrocnemius contracture compares dorsiflexion of the ankle with
the knee flexed and then extended. The test is performed with the patient seated on the
examination table facing the examiner. The hindfoot is held in inversion to lock the
transverse tarsal joints, and maximum ankle dorsiflexion is evaluated. Because the
gastrocnemius crosses the knee joint, contracture of that muscle will limit ankle
dorsiflexion with the knee in full extension but not in flexion. If the patient has an
isolated soleus contracture, it will not affect ankle dorsiflexion with the knee flexed or
extended because the soleus originates at the posterior tibia and does not cross the
knee joint (Video 4).

To test Achilles tendon integrity, examine the patient in the prone position. Missed
Achilles tendon ruptures are a source of multiple medical malpractice claims. To perform
the Thompson test, the patient is placed in the prone position, the knee is flexed to 90°,
and the calf is squeezed firmly at the area of maximum girth of the gastrocnemius
muscle. A test is positive if no ankle plantar flexion occurs with this maneuver, indicating
tendon discontinuity. The examiner also should perform this test on the opposite
uninjured extremity. This often is confusing in documentation; therefore, dictating the
finding and whether the test is positive or negative is the best method to communicate
the state of the tendon. In patients with a negative Thompson test, dictation would state
that the test was negative because squeezing the calf resulted in a normal degree of
ankle plantar flexion, indicating that the Achilles tendon is in continuity (Video 7). In
patient with a positive Thompson test, dictation would state that the test was positive
because squeezing the calf muscle did not result in a normal degree of ankle plantar
flexion, indicating that the Achilles tendon is not in continuity (Video 8). In general, a gap
is noted 5 to 8 cm proximal to the Achilles tendon insertion during palpation; however,
rupture at the insertion is more difficult to assess via this method (Video 9).
Video 7 Faro FD: Video. Negative Thompson and Matles Test. Lebanon, NH, 2023.

To perform the Matles test for relative resting position of the foot, the patient is placed
in the prone position, both knees are flexed to 90°, and the plantar surfaces of the feet
are evaluated. If the suspected injured foot has the same degree of resting plantar
flexion as the uninjured side, then the Achilles tendon is in continuity at its normal

other indicates lengthening or interruption of the tendon. In a neglected rupture that
has healed, no gap may be palpable because it has been replaced by scar tissue. The
scar fills the void left by the ruptured tendon and effectively lengthens the tendon
(Figure 2).

In the Coleman block test for hindfoot flexibility in the cavus foot, the patient stands with
the lateral side of the affected foot placed on a support three-quarters of an inch thick (a
block or a book). The great toe and the first metatarsal head/shaft are suspended and
allowed to sag or plantarflex maximally off the object. If hindfoot varus corrects (viewed
posteriorly), the existing hindfoot varus deformity is deemed flexible, and the cavus foot
deformity is driven by a forefoot valgus deformity (rigid plantar flexion or a humpback
deformity) rather than the hindfoot (Video 10).

The test for peroneal tendon subluxation is performed with the patient seated on the
examination table facing the examiner. With the foot in an inverted position, the patient
attempts to evert the foot against resistance of the examiner. An unstable peroneal
tendon will subluxate over the posterior distal fibula, eliciting a positive response (Video
11).

During palpation for posterior tibialis tendon pathology, note thickening and/or
tenderness along the course of the tendon, particularly posterior to the medial malleolus
at the location at which the tendon courses at a 70° angle. The heel rise test for posterior
tibialis tendon pathology is performed with the patient standing and the examiner
viewing the motion of the heels. Ensure that any support for the patient is to the side so
the patient cannot launch forward, powering their elevation with the gastrocsoleus
complex. This compensatory motion will not result in heel inversion but may trick the
examiner into thinking posterior tibial function is intact. Patients with a torn or
dysfunctional tendon will not be able to perform a single heel rise on the affected side
(Video 12). The examiner notes a lack of inversion on the affected side with the double
heel rise (Video 13). Pain along the course of the tendon with the single leg heel rise also
is a sign of tendon pathology. Patients without a substantial tendon length discrepancy
and patients with tendinosis will be unable to perform as many single heel rises on the
affected side as that on the unaffected side; this test is referred to as the repetitive
single heel rise test.

The piano key test for Lisfranc injury is used to evaluate the tarsometatarsal joints. The
midfoot is stabilized, and the examiner grasps the metatarsal heads and moves them
individually into dorsiflexion and plantar flexion (Video 14). In addition, the first

metatarsal is moved into abduction. Pain at the tarsometatarsal joints indicates
pathology and complements the radiographic evaluation to define the specific
tarsometatarsal joints involved.
Video 14 Faro FD: Video. Piano Key Test for Lisfranc Stability. Lebanon, NH, 2023.
To determine the forefoot-hindfoot relationship, the ankle is placed in neutral, the
calcaneus is placed in line with the tibia, and the talonavicular joint is placed in neutral
(the talar head is covered by the navicular); the position of the forefoot is then evaluated.
If the great toe and the metatarsal cascade are in varus (elevated in relation to the plane
of the posterior plantar surface of the foot), then the patient has a pronated foot. If the
opposite is true and the forefoot is in valgus (depressed relative to the posterior plantar
surface of the foot), then the patient has a supinated foot.
The squeeze test for interdigital (Morton) neuroma may be used to evaluate for an
interdigital (Morton) neuroma. The examiner performs this test by applying dorsoplantar
pressure within the designated webspace by pinching with the thumb and forefinger and
then applying mediolateral pressure across the metatarsal head with the other hand.
Pain radiating out the toes as mediolateral pressure is applied indicates a positive test. If
the neuroma involves more severe bursitis or swelling around the involved nerve, a
palpable click (Mulder sign) will occur as the neuroma is displaced from between the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:44 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000027
22/25

metatarsal heads during the squeeze test. The examiner can attempt to provocatively
elicit the Mulder sign click by first applying superior pressure with the thumb at the site
of the neuroma (delivering it into the webspace) and then applying the metatarsal
squeeze with the fingers medial/lateral. This maneuver may then push the neuroma out
of the webspace, creating the click (Video 15).
Video 15 Faro FD: Video. Squeeze Test for Morton Neuroma. Lebanon, NH, 2023.
To test for metatarsophalangeal joint dislocation, dorsal palpation at the
metatarsophalangeal joints may be revealing. With dorsal subluxation or dislocation at
the metatarsophalangeal joints, the ridge of the base of the proximal phalanx often can
be appreciated. This ridge also may be observed in patients with a longstanding hallux
valgus deformity or after trauma or inflammatory arthropathy. Stabilizing the metatarsal
head with one hand by pinching it between the thumb and forefinger and then
translating the proximal phalanx forward may reveal instability or elicit pain indicating
arthropathy or a plantar plate injury (Video 16).
